historic_survey.note: Listed among the five designated San Francisco Landmarks in the study area, as Landmark #264. The statement dates the building to 1901 and its Mediterranean Revival restyling to 1923. It gives the tavern's address as 401 Castro Street where it lists the landmarks, and as 410 Castro Street where it quotes the citywide LGBTQ context statement — 410 being the Bank of America branch across the intersection.

building.name: Twin Peaks Tavern
building.completed_conflict: The assessor's roll gives 1901; the 2012 Article 10 landmark case report dates the building to 1883.

historical_record.description: Built as a saloon and cigar store, which it was trading as by the 1890s.

A quarrel over an unpaid round of drinks ended in a gun battle across the saloon's pool table, in which the proprietor was shot dead; the charge against the other man was dismissed six weeks later on the testimony that the proprietor had fired first.
Victorian trim and a second storey added.

Raided by federal agents as part of a sweep of forty premises. A foot switch dropped the liquor supply through a trapdoor onto bricks in the cellar; the crash gave the raid away, forty gallons of alcohol were seized as evidence and the saloon keeper was arrested after offering the agents $65.
The exterior remade in Mediterranean revival style, and largely as it was left then.

The Twin Peaks Tavern, on this corner since 1935, was bought by two lesbian owners who installed large plate-glass windows, making what has been described as the first gay bar in the United States with a street-visible interior.
